This medRxiv preprint, which has not been peer-reviewed, examines antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Enterobacteriaceae from untreated wastewater in Western Uttar Pradesh (WUP), India, during the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors report that the pandemic increased antibiotic use in India, including about 216.4 million additional doses. They also note that inadequate wastewater treatment allows resistant bacteria to enter the environment.

Fifteen wastewater samples were collected in triplicate in 2020–2021 from three zones covering metropolitan and non-metropolitan cities. Isolates were identified biochemically and with VITEK2. They were tested against 19 antibiotics in eight classes, and screened for extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) production and colistin resistance.

Of 150 isolates:
- 62% were E. coli, 24% K. pneumoniae, 8% other Enterobacteriaceae and 6% mixed populations.
- 74% resisted one or more antibiotics, and 79.3% of these produced ESBL.
- Multidrug resistance (MDR) occurred in E. coli (57.14%), K. pneumoniae (28.57%) and Pantoea agglomerans (5.71%).

Zone 1 had the highest MDR overall and for K. pneumoniae, while Zone 3 had the most MDR E. coli. Zonal differences in total MDR were not significant (p=0.85). However, K. pneumoniae MDR prevalence was significantly higher than that of E. coli (p=0.0081). Carbapenem resistance was 37–59%, and combined ciprofloxacin resistance was 67.5%. Colistin resistance was detected, including in Pantoea spp., which the authors describe as a first report for the region.

The authors conclude that MDR was similar in metropolitan and non-metropolitan cities. They link the resistance to antibiotic misuse during the pandemic and to untreated wastewater disposal, noting that about 75% of wastewater in non-metropolitan cities is untreated. They call for policy attention, infrastructure upgrades, periodic AMR surveillance and molecular studies of resistance genes.

**Power supply decoupling:** PLL and analog supplies need a ferrite bead with at least one capacitor on the device side, ideally forming a Pi filter placed close to the pin. Decoupling capacitors should be 0.1 µF, no larger than 0402. Place at least one per two power pins, plus a 10 µF or larger bulk capacitor per roughly 10 pins. Too much capacitance can slow voltage ramps and alter power sequencing.

**Resets:** The device supports several reset types:
- **Power-on Reset (POR):** A cold reset of the entire chip, including emulation logic and the EMAC Switch. POR stays low until supplies and clocks are stable. On release, BTMODE[15:0] is latched and the ARM Cortex-A8 executes from Boot ROM.
- **External Warm Reset (RESET pin):** Resets everything except test/emulation logic, PLL and clock configuration, and optionally the EMAC Switch.
- **Other resets:** Emulation warm, watchdog, software global cold/warm (via PRM_RSTCTRL), test (TRST), and local module resets each have specific variations.
- **Priority and status:** Simultaneous resets are handled by priority, and PRM_RSTST records the last reset.
- **Isolation:** PCIe can be reset independently. The EMAC Switch can stay active during all resets except POR when ISO_CONTROL is set.
- **RSTOUT_WD_OUT:** Reflects reset status, is always asserted on watchdog reset, and depends on BTMODE[11] otherwise.
- **Pin states and power domains:** Most I/Os enter Hi-Z during reset, with exceptions for emulation, EMAC Switch, and DDR pins. Each power domain has dedicated warm and cold resets.

**Clocking:**
- **DEV and AUX clocks:** Sourced from crystals with internal oscillators or from 1.8-V LVCMOS inputs. DEV is normally 20 MHz (20–30 MHz under certain conditions). AUX is optional at 20–30 MHz.
- **SERDES clock:** The PCIe PHY needs a low-jitter, AC-coupled differential clock.
- **Optional inputs and outputs:** CLKIN32 (32768 Hz) and AUD_CLKIN0/1/2 (max 50 MHz) are optional inputs. CLKOUT0/1 are selectable outputs.
- **PLLs:** There are 12 top-level and 4 embedded PLLs, all starting in Bypass mode after reset. They must respect multiplier, divider, and frequency limits, and PLL_USB must be 960 MHz when USB is used. SYSCLKs and module clocks have maximum frequencies.

**Interrupts:** The ARM interrupt controller (AINTC) handles up to 128 requests. The C674x DSP controller combines 128 events into 12 prioritized interrupts, with multiplexing options.

**Timing conventions:** Specified timings exclude board routing delays, and TI recommends IBIS models for analysis. 3.3-V I/O uses Vref = 1.5 V.

**Peripherals:**
- **DCAN:** Two CAN 2.0 A/B interfaces.
- **EDMA:** 64 channels, mappable to 512 parameter entries.
- **Debug:** Advanced Event Triggering, Trace, and IEEE 1149.1 JTAG (JTAG ID 0x0B8F202F; TRST has an internal pulldown).
- **EMAC Switch:** 3-port gigabit switch with two external ports supporting MII/GMII/RMII/RGMII. I/O is 3.3 V only, plus MDIO for PHY management.
- **GPIO:** Up to 128 pins in four modules with interrupt capability.
- **GPMC:** Interfaces to NOR/NAND Flash, SRAM, and Pseudo-SRAM with 512 MB addressing. The ELM provides BCH error location.
- **HDMI:** 1.3a-compliant transmitter. TMDS routing requires 100 Ω differential and 60 Ω single-ended impedance, and ESD protection must stay at or below 5 pF.
- **HDVPSS:** Video input/output processing with HD/SD encoders and graphics layers.
- **Video DAC:** Normal or TVOUT Bypass mode, with specific layout guidelines.
- **I2C:** Four modules compliant with I2C specification 2.1, supporting 10–400 Kbps.

This excerpt from Texas Instruments' TMS320DM814x DaVinci Digital Media Processors documentation covers reset, clocking, interrupts and peripheral specifications.

**Reset**
- **PCIE reset isolation:** The PCIE Subsystem can be reset without resetting the rest of the device.
  - As Root Complex, software resets it through the PRCM after placing it in IDLE, then re-enumerates the bus.
  - As Endpoint, an in-band reset generates an interrupt that software handles by idling the subsystem and asserting a local reset.
- **EMAC Switch reset isolation:** When the ISO_CONTROL bit in the RESET_ISO register is set, the switch can keep routing traffic through all resets except POR. Its PLL, some Control Module registers and some pin multiplexing are preserved.
- **RSTOUT_WD_OUT pin:** This pin reflects reset status and is always asserted on a Watchdog reset. It is also asserted on POR and External Warm Reset if BTMODE[11] is latched as "0".
- **Power domain resets:** Each power domain has dedicated Warm and Cold Resets, triggered by global resets or by switching between ON and OFF states.
- **Pin behavior at reset:** Most I/O pins enter Hi-Z, with exceptions for emulation, EMAC Switch, RSTOUT_WD_OUT and DDR pins. After reset, the Boot ROM reconfigures the PINCNTL registers.

**Clocking**
- **DEV and AUX clocks:** Both can come from an external crystal with the internal oscillator or from a 1.8-V LVCMOS clock input.
  - DEV is normally 20 MHz and may range up to 30 MHz under specific conditions.
  - AUX is optional, ranges from 20 to 30 MHz, and can source the Audio and Video PLLs.
- **PCIE PHY clock:** Requires a low-jitter, AC-coupled differential SERDES clock.
- **Optional clock inputs:** CLKIN32 and AUD_CLKIN0–2 (50 MHz maximum).
- **Clock outputs:** Two selectable outputs, CLKOUT0 and CLKOUT1.
- **PLLs:** The device has 12 top-level PLLs and 4 embedded PLLs, all starting in Bypass mode after reset. PLL_USB must be 960 MHz when USB is used.
- **Frequency limits:** Maximum SYSCLK and module clock frequencies are specified.

**Interrupts and EDMA**
- **ARM Cortex-A8 interrupts:** The AINTC handles up to 128 requests.
- **C674x DSP interrupts:** The DSP controller combines 128 events into 12 prioritized interrupts, with multiplexing options.
- **EDMA:** Supports 64 channels mappable to 512 parameter entries.

**Timing and Debug**
- **Timing references:** AC timing uses defined test loads and reference levels. Board routing delays are excluded, and IBIS models are recommended.
- **Debug features:** Advanced Event Triggering, Trace, and IEEE 1149.1 JTAG. The JTAG ID register value is 0x0B8F202F.

**Peripherals**
- **DCAN:** Two interfaces supporting CAN 2.0 A/B.
- **EMAC Switch:**
  - 3-port gigabit switch with two external ports supporting MII, GMII, RMII and RGMII.
  - Uses 3.3-V I/O only.
  - Includes an MDIO interface for PHY management.
- **GPIO:** Up to 128 pins across four modules.
- **GPMC/ELM:** Supports NOR/NAND Flash and SRAM with up to 512 MB addressing. The ELM provides BCH error location.
- **HDMI:** 1.3a-compliant transmitter, with TMDS routing requiring 100-Ω differential impedance and an ESD protection chip.
- **HDVPSS:** Video processing, display and capture.
- **Video DACs:** Operate in Normal or TVOUT Bypass mode, with layout guidelines.
- **I2C:** Four modules operating at 10–400 Kbps.
- **Imaging Subsystem:** CAM and CSI2 interfaces feeding the ISP.
- **DDR2/DDR3 controllers:** Two interfaces with 16- or 32-bit data paths, governed by routing specifications and rules for handling unused pins.

Out of bounds situations are a major part of basketball, and teams must be prepared to inbound the ball from the baseline, sideline and full court. Whatever the coaching philosophy, the main goal is to inbound successfully and get the ball to the best players for a high-percentage shot. Plays should be simple and practiced beforehand, since new plays drawn up during timeouts rarely succeed. Inbounders need fundamental skills and a commitment to team play, because a turnover creates a five-on-four disadvantage.

Successful plays depend on vision, communication, execution, timing and reading the defense. Automatic reads, such as back-door cuts, give-and-go passes and lob passes, are the first option. Teams should scout opponents beforehand or during the game.

Players must know key rules:
- The ball must be released within five seconds.
- The inbounder cannot be changed once designated and cannot touch the ball until another player does.
- The inbounder may move along the baseline only after a made shot.
- Passing into the backcourt is legal.
- Throwing the ball over the backboard or directly into the basket is illegal.
- A defender reaching across the boundary plane to touch the ball is a technical foul.

Coaches are advised to test players' rule knowledge.

This qualitative study by Zafer Kuş and Hilal Mert examines the links between science education and citizenship education in Turkey. It addresses two questions: what aspects of citizenship education the Turkish science curriculum includes, and how science teachers view and foster their role in citizenship education.

**Background:** Citizenship education has evolved beyond building national identity toward preparing informed, active, and responsible citizens, both nationally and globally. The literature links science education to citizenship through scientific literacy, socio-scientific issues, Science-Technology-Society-Environment (STSE) topics, and the Sustainable Development Goals. In Turkey, citizenship education was briefly treated as multidisciplinary in 2005. From 2010–2011, it became a standalone 4th-grade course, with social studies responsible for it at the secondary level. This separated it from science education. The 2018 science curriculum is based on STSE and emphasizes scientific, technological, and environmental literacy, but its connection to citizenship education remains weak and under-researched.

**Method:** The researchers analyzed the science curriculum for grades 5–8 and conducted semi-structured interviews with eight experienced science teachers. They used thematic analysis with Maxqda software.

**Findings:** Seven themes emerged:
- **Scientific literacy:** Teachers saw scientific literacy as essential for active citizenship.
- **Technology:** Teachers drew only weak links between technology and citizenship.
- **Society:** The curriculum and teachers connected science to daily life, health, safety, civic responsibilities, and socio-scientific issues such as COVID-19, climate change, and GMOs.
- **Environment:** This was the most prominent theme in both the curriculum and the interviews, with teachers tying active citizenship to environmental protection.
- **Values and skills:** Values included responsibility, respect, and patriotism. Skills included observation, inquiry, critical thinking, and problem-solving.
- **Problems:** Teachers reported that, in practice, science education falls short of its citizenship goals. Causes included overcrowded classrooms, inadequate laboratories and materials, an exam-oriented system, curriculum shortcomings, and difficulties with student readiness, parents, and refugee students.

**Conclusions:** Science classes have potential to strengthen citizenship competencies. The authors recommend that policymakers explicitly emphasize citizenship skills in the science curriculum and promote socio-scientific and environmental topics. They also call for teacher training and a citizenship-oriented approach to science education aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals.

Artificial intelligence enables personalized education, and early AI literacy is increasingly seen as part of digital competence. Educational robots are used from preschool onward, including for inclusion and for supporting children with autism spectrum disorder. Serbia's *Years of Ascent* Preschool Curriculum Framework (2018), alongside UNESCO, EU, and Serbian strategies, emphasizes digital competence. This makes it important to understand how future teachers perceive robots.

**Method**
- **Approach:** Using a mixed-method approach modeled on the Draw-A-Robot Test, researchers asked fourth-year students at the University of Belgrade's Faculty of Education to draw a robot and explain its setting, role, and why they chose it.
- **Coding:** Responses were coded with a DAAT checklist. Inter-rater agreement was 0.99.
- **Sample:** Of 143 participants, 22 showed misconceptions. The final sample was 121 students: 75 future preschool teachers and 46 future primary teachers.

**Results**
- **Misconceptions:** Most of the 22 misconceptions (68.18%) depicted robots as electrical appliances. Others showed stick figures, VR hardware, or avatars.
- **Experience:** Most participants had real-life experience with robots (98), and 21 knew them through media. Future preschool teachers had about three times more in-person experience, possibly because of their curriculum.
- **Appearance:** Animal-shaped robots, especially Bee-Bot, were most common (47.1%), followed by typical robots (24.8%), mechanical objects (24.0%), and humanoids (4.1%).
- **Emotion:** Most robots showed no emotion (76), 44 showed positive emotion, and one showed negative emotion.
- **Functions:** Robots were mainly assigned educational (52.9%) or assistive (31.4%) functions. Preschool students emphasized the educational function, while primary students weighted educational and assistive functions equally.
- **Where seen:** Most participants first encountered robots at the Faculty of Education (61).
- **Reasons for choice:** Choices reflected the cognitive domain (33.9%), affective domain (23.1%), and behavioral domain (16.5%). For 26.4%, the reason could not be determined.

**Conclusion**
Most future teachers hold accurate conceptions of robots. Future preschool teachers showed more consistent conceptions and prioritized the cognitive domain. The authors recommend more frequent, purposeful use of educational robots, revised syllabuses, and dedicated curriculum teams. They also stress attention to children's safety, privacy, and equal access.

In this lecture, Markus Klute discusses experimental studies of neutrino oscillations. Neutrino sources include supernovae, Big Bang relics (which have very low energies and are hard to observe), cosmic ray showers, the sun, accelerators, and nuclear reactors. Neutrinos can also be used to monitor nuclear activity worldwide. Key experimental parameters are distance, energy, and sensitivity to a mass range.

**Solar neutrinos**
- Early experiments, such as the Davis/Homestake chlorine-tank experiment, detected fewer electron neutrinos than theory predicted.
- The SNO experiment used neutral scattering to measure the total neutrino count and found it agreed with expectations.
- This showed that the neutrinos change flavor rather than disappear, providing the first evidence of solar neutrino oscillation.

**Atmospheric neutrinos**
- These come from pion and kaon decays in cosmic ray interactions, which predict a muon-to-electron neutrino ratio of about 2.
- This ratio was not observed. Zenith-angle measurements showed that muon neutrinos disappear.

**Accelerator neutrinos**
- Facilities at Fermilab (NuMI), CERN, and Japan use a near detector to measure total flux and a far detector to study appearance or disappearance.
- T2K data clearly show oscillation.

**Reactor neutrinos**
- These are produced by fission of heavy isotopes, with flux calculated from thermal power or fuel use.
- Experiments study anti-electron neutrino disappearance via inverse beta decay.
- Survival probability plotted against length over energy directly shows oscillation.

Accelerator and reactor studies expanded significantly in the 2000s.

The Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR), characterized by artificial intelligence and machine learning, is expected to strongly affect education. India's National Education Policy 2020 stresses foundational, higher-order, social and emotional skills and flexible learning paths. It recommends games and gamification as an innovative pedagogy. Education 4.0 requires shifting from rote learning to personalized learning and from memory-based to skill-based assessment.

**Digital games in teaching and learning**
Digital games can develop cognitive and non-cognitive skills, increase motivation, and provide immersive, enjoyable learning. Their elements, such as challenges, rules, goals, immediate feedback and multiple solutions, align with good instructional design. Digital Game Based Learning (DGBL) uses either existing commercial games or customized games aligned with learning outcomes. Studies link DGBL to academic achievement, motivation and higher-order skills.

**Digital games in assessment**
Traditional assessments are often detached from learning and face validity issues. Digital games can serve as flexible, adaptive assessment tools that measure both procedural and declarative knowledge.

**Stealth Assessment (SA)**
Stealth Assessment, a term first used by Valerie Shute, evaluates learners during gameplay without their awareness. Machine learning algorithms analyze gameplay data to infer competencies, provide immediate feedback, and assign new challenges matched to each learner. This approach reduces test anxiety while maintaining validity. SA depends on:
- **Evidence Centered Design (ECD):** a multidisciplinary approach that defines which competencies to measure and how, and collects only relevant evidence.
- **Machine learning algorithms:** these collect, link and statistically analyze evidence.
- **Formative feedback:** results are used to support further learning.

Under this model, pedagogy designs the activities and interprets the results, while the algorithms process the gameplay evidence.

**Challenges**
- DGBL remains underused due to doubts about its efficiency.
- Developing customized games requires expertise from multiple disciplines.
- Some research raises concerns about gaming's effects on the brain.
- Games can impose cognitive load, and poorly calibrated difficulty can cause learners to disengage.
- Establishing the validity and reliability of DGBL is still at an early stage and requires extensive research.

A penalty kick awarded during play is a restart, and the ball is live once kicked. Attacking players must be pre-positioned and react to saves, blocks, or rebounds by moving toward goal to shoot. Under Law 14, all players except the kicker and goalkeeper must be at least 10 yards from the penalty mark, behind it, inside the field, and outside the Penalty Area. Players should take positions immediately, hold their ground if jostled, and enter the area only after the ball is kicked and clearly moves forward, not at the referee's signal. The kicker may not touch the ball again until another player does, such as a goalkeeper block, but not a rebound off the goal. Alex Morgan's hesitation after a blocked kick against Vietnam in the 2023 Women's World Cup illustrates a lost chance. Teammates must pursue the ball without hesitation, and switch to defense if the goalkeeper secures it. Violations result in a retake or an indirect free kick.

This discussion paper argues that growing government regulation of AI will significantly affect AI development, yet AI policy is largely absent from computer science curricula. The authors synthesize US and EU regulatory developments and propose a framework for integrating AI policy discussions into CS courses.

**US and EU landscape:** The US lacks comprehensive federal AI legislation and relies on non-binding statements. State and federal policy shows partisan divides. President Biden's EO 14110, which emphasized safe and trustworthy AI, was rescinded by President Trump, whose EO 14179 prioritizes "global AI dominance," economic competitiveness, and national security. The EU AI Act, approved in March 2024, defines AI systems broadly and classifies them by risk. It prohibits "unacceptable risk" practices and imposes transparency requirements on general-purpose models.

**Key themes:**
- US AI policy is volatile, so developers familiar with the policy landscape will adapt better.
- Abstract policy goals must be translated into technical controls, and some requirements, such as uncircumventable watermarks, lack technical solutions.
- EU rules may shape global practice, as the GDPR did through the "Brussels Effect."

**Framework:** The framework spans three perspectives: socio-political, translational, and technical. These intersect with three dimensions:
- **Scope:** what a policy requires or prohibits, and of whom.
- **Power:** who creates and benefits from a policy.
- **Agency:** how practitioners can influence policy.

A grid of guiding questions embodies the framework, which is flexible across curricula. Suggested future work includes linking the framework to specific curricular activities and applying requirements engineering to the "principles to practices" gap.

Researchers developed and experimentally validated a multiscale framework that links atomic-scale energetics at the GaN–Ga melt interface to macroscopic growth kinetics in self-catalyzed molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE).

**Interface structure:** Molecular dynamics simulations using a machine learning interatomic potential showed that liquid Ga forms ordered layers at the GaN interface at 1000 K.
- Ordering is longer-ranged at Ga-polar interfaces than at N-polar interfaces.
- Charge redistribution is confined to the first one or two layers.

**N adatom energetics:** Metadynamics simulations mapped free energy landscapes for N adatom adsorption and migration, which correspond to the liquid Ga layering.
- Lateral migration barriers were about 0.56 eV (Ga-polar) and 0.34 eV (N-polar), compared with about 1.1 eV on a clean Ga-polar surface.
- This "Ga lubrication" mechanism explains the catalytic role of Ga droplets.
- Step-edge (Ehrlich-Schwoebel) barriers exceeded 0.6 eV.

**Growth mode:** Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations parameterized with these barriers showed two flux-dependent regimes.
- High N flux produced rough, island-like growth.
- Lower flux produced layer-by-layer growth.
- Under practical MBE fluxes, which are lower still, growth is expected to be diffusion-controlled and smooth.

**Growth-rate model:** A diffusion model based on a modified Fick's law used simulated free energy profiles, N diffusivity, and N solubility, with no fitted parameters. It predicted facet-dependent growth rates of 0.01–0.04 nm/s.

**Experimental validation:** Ga droplets were nitridated by MBE for 1 and 5 minutes, and more than 200 particles were analyzed by electron microscopy.
- Mean GaN radii were about 3–7 nm at 1 minute and 10–15 nm at 5 minutes.
- Observed trends matched predictions, such as faster growth of the m-plane than the basal planes.

**Significance:** Unlike P and As in other III-V systems, N has very low solubility in Ga. Nitride growth is therefore governed by interfacial free energy profiles rather than bulk droplet chemistry. The workflow is described as transferable to other low-solubility systems.

**Limitations:**
- Impurities were not considered.
- The interatomic potential has limited accuracy for some configurations.
- The model relies on simplifying assumptions.
- Experimental data average over multiple facets.

Graphene and 5G, both accused of hype, may help each other's prospects, according to developments shown at the Graphene Pavilion at Mobile World Congress in Barcelona. - **Graphene-based ICs:** RWTH Aachen University and AMO GmbH developed a flexible graphene microwave receiver and transmitter for Wi-Fi and mmWave uses. It performs comparably to, or better than, costly gallium arsenide at lower cost. Flagship director Jari Kinaret said yield and material consistency remain obstacles.
- **Cryogenic cooling:** Chalmers University and APR Technologies created a graphene-based miniature cooling pump with no moving parts. It could cool receivers in 5G base stations.
- **Graphene photonics:** A CNIT-led collaboration with AMO, Ericsson, Nokia Bell Labs and Imec produced graphene photodetectors and modulators. They are 10 times more efficient than silicon devices, and Ericsson demonstrated a 100 Gbps channel based on the technology.

Kinaret said the remaining challenges are mainly in manufacturing, with "no showstoppers."

In soccer, once the first defender controls the opponent with the ball, a second "support" or "cover" defender positions themself goalside, behind and inside the first defender. This forces the dribbler toward the sideline and lets the support defender react if the first defender is beaten. The support defender uses the same stance, keeps an appropriate distance without overrunning the play, and adjusts to the first defender's movements.

Communication is critical because the first defender faces away and cannot see the field. The support defender:
- Announces arrival ("support," "you have help").
- Calls "jockey" or "contain" to buy time for teammates to return.
- Calls "tackle" or "take him" when ready to cover.

Instruction progresses from a stationary demonstration near the halfway line to relative movement, then half-speed with communication, then full speed. If the first defender is beaten, the support defender likely takes over, possibly through a "Defensive Switch."

This excerpt from the Texas Instruments ADS8681W/ADS8685W/ADS8689W (ADS868xW) data sheet covers the device's analog front end, digital interface, registers, application guidance, and support information.

**Analog Front End**
- **Programmable gain amplifier (PGA):** Converts single-ended or differential inputs to drive the internal SAR ADC and adjusts the common-mode level to maximize dynamic range.
  - Gain is set with the RANGE_SEL[3:0] bits. The default is 0000, which gives ±3 × VREF.
  - Trimmed, matched resistors keep gain error low.
- **Low-pass filter:** A second-order antialiasing filter at the PGA output reduces noise, with a typical –3dB cutoff of 500kHz.
- **ADC driver:** An integrated high-bandwidth, low-noise buffer charges the sample-and-hold capacitors.

**Reference**
- The INTREF_DIS bit selects the reference. The internal reference is enabled by default.
- **Internal reference (4.096V):**
  - Requires at least a 4.7µF capacitor between REFIO and REFGND.
  - REFIO should not drive external loads unless it is buffered.
  - Accuracy can shift due to mechanical or thermal stress, particularly solder reflow. On boards with multiple reflows, the device should be soldered in the second pass.
  - The reference is temperature compensated from –40°C to +125°C.
- **External reference (4.096V):**
  - Applied at REFIO and driven through an internal buffer to REFCAP.
  - REFCAP requires 10µF and 1µF capacitors.
  - Buffer drift is typically 0.5ppm/°C, with a maximum of 2ppm/°C.

**Transfer Function**
- Output uses straight-binary format for bipolar and unipolar ranges.
- LSB size equals FSR/2¹⁶.

**Alarms**
- The ALARM/SDO-1/GPO pin provides an active-high alarm output when SDO1_CONFIG = 01b.
- **Input alarm:** Uses programmable high and low thresholds with shared hysteresis.
- **AVDD alarm:** Uses fixed thresholds of 4.7V and 5.3V.
- Each alarm has active and tripped flags:
  - Active flags clear after each conversion.
  - Tripped flags clear when ALARM_REG is read.
- Flags can be read through the pin, the registers, or appended to output data.

**Operating Modes and Interface**
- **multiSPI interface:** The host sees the device as a 32-bit shift register.
- **Connection topologies:** All multiSPI options, standard SPI, and daisy-chain.
  - In daisy-chain mode, all devices use identical configurations.
  - An optimal frame has 32 × N SCLK edges.
  - Throughput decreases as more devices are added.
- **Device states:** RESET, ACQ, and CONV.
  - RST can act as either a power-on reset or an application reset, selected by the RSTn_APP bit.
  - Conversion uses an internal clock, and the host monitors RVS or waits for tconv_max.

**Programming**
- **Frame length:**
  - Exactly 32 SCLKs makes an optimal frame.
  - Fewer than 32 makes a short frame, which writes as a no-operation command, though the output data remains valid.
  - More than 32 makes a long frame, where the last 32 bits form the command.
- **Commands:** Include byte and half-word (HWORD) read, write, set, and clear operations. The address LSB is ignored for HWORD commands.
- **Output word:** Contains conversion data, register data, or a fixed pattern. Optional flags include device address, range, alarm flags, and parity.
- **Protocols:**
  - Four SPI modes are available for writing. SPI-00-S is the default.
  - Reading supports single or dual SDO and source-synchronous (SRC) modes with an internal or external clock.

**Registers**
- Nine configuration registers are covered: device ID, reset/power control (write-protected by key 69h), SDI and SDO control, data output control, range selection, alarm flags, and alarm thresholds.

**Application Example**
- An 8-channel PLC analog input module pairs the ADS8681W with the MUX36D08 multiplexer.
  - The ADS868xW settles to 1% in under 5µs.
  - It handles inputs up to ±12.288V.
- An NTC thermistor example illustrates input alarm thresholds, with hysteresis preventing false triggering.

**Power and Layout**
- **Supplies:** Separate AVDD and DVDD supplies, with recommended decoupling capacitors that improve PSRR.
- **Low-power modes:** NAP and power-down (PD), both enabled through RST_PWRCTL_REG.
- **Layout:** Separate analog and digital sections, keep bypass capacitors close to pins, and avoid vias between pins and capacitors.

**Supporting Information**
- Related documents, support resources, trademarks, and an ESD caution.
- Revision A (May 2025) changed the ADS8685W and ADS8689W to Production Data.
- Packaging notes and TI disclaimers.

This qualitative case study examines the legal frameworks guiding inclusive education and educational leaders' awareness of them in inclusive education resource centers in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. The authors note that earlier research, such as Girma (2017), focused on barriers like infrastructure and teacher preparedness rather than on legal frameworks and leaders' awareness of them.

**Methods**

The study involved fifteen purposively selected participants:
- School principals, itinerant teachers and teachers from three resource centers
- Experts from the Ministry of Education's Inclusion Department

Data came from semi-structured interviews and reviews of policy documents, and were analyzed thematically.

**Legal frameworks identified**

- **Global:** the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, ICERD, the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the Salamanca Statement, the CRPD, the Marrakesh Treaty and the SDGs.
- **Regional:** the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, and the African Disability Protocol (2018).
- **National:** the Ethiopian Constitution, Proclamation No. 1263/2021, the Education and Training Policy (2023), ESDP VI (2020–2025), the Special Needs/Inclusive Education Strategy (2022/23–2029/30) and the National Children's Policy (2017).

**Awareness findings**

- **Ministry experts** showed knowledge of international and national frameworks. One noted that Ethiopia lacks a specific, stand-alone inclusive education policy.
- **Principals** reported limited or no knowledge of these frameworks, citing minimal training and daily workloads.
- **Itinerant teachers**, who have special needs education backgrounds, demonstrated good awareness. They observed that many principals and district leaders lack such awareness and inclusive education training.
- **Teachers** were unaware of any legal frameworks and viewed inclusion mainly as a matter of compassion and fairness.

**Conclusions and recommendations**

The study concludes that the policy environment is favorable, but awareness varies among leaders, possibly due to differences in qualifications and training. It recommends:
- Regular professional development on inclusive education policies
- Integrating these frameworks into teacher training curricula
- Ministry-level monitoring and enhancement of practitioners' policy awareness

This study compared air-conduction (AC) and bone-conduction (BC) auditory brainstem response (ABR) and auditory steady-state response (ASSR) thresholds in infants aged 0–6 months. Infants had either normal hearing (NH) or conductive hearing loss (CHL), with groups defined by ABR, the current gold standard for early hearing detection and intervention (EHDI) programs. The authors note that peer-reviewed data comparing BC ASSR to BC ABR in young infants with hearing loss were lacking.

**Methods**
- Sixty-four infants who failed or missed newborn screening at the Royal University Hospital, Saskatoon, participated. Fourteen were excluded because they did not sleep.
- Each frequency was classified as NH or CHL using British Columbia Early Hearing Program (BCEHP) ABR criteria. Tympanometry and otoacoustic emissions served as cross-checks.
- ABR used BCEHP tone stimuli. ASSR used four simultaneous AM2 tones presented to one ear.
- Testing proceeded down to threshold in 10-dB steps.
- No CHL occurred at 2000 Hz, so analyses focused on 500 Hz.

**Results**
- AC ABR and ASSR thresholds were significantly higher in the CHL group. BC thresholds did not differ between groups.
- ABR and ASSR thresholds were not correlated.
- Mean 500-Hz air-bone gaps (ABGs) were:
  - ABR: 15 dB (NH) and 36 dB (CHL)
  - ASSR: 12 dB (NH) and 21 dB (CHL)
- Both methods showed significantly larger ABGs in CHL, but ASSR showed more overlap between groups.
- Minimum normal intensities:
  - ABR: 35/20 dB nHL (500 Hz AC/BC) and 30/30 dB nHL (2000 Hz)
  - ASSR: 40/30 dB HL (500 Hz) and 40/40 dB HL (2000 Hz)
- Screening tests had high sensitivity but poor specificity. ASSR cutoffs with high sensitivity lacked high specificity.

**Discussion and limitations**
Threshold differences may reflect calibration differences, offset starting levels, step size, mild CHL, sample size, and stimulus differences. ABGs were judged more appropriate as descriptive rather than singular diagnostic tools. Limitations included:
- CHL that was mild and present only at 500 Hz
- No infants with sensorineural hearing loss
- A single response judge
- No acoustic reflex testing
- ABR always tested before ASSR
- No correction factors applied

**Conclusion**
ASSR variability was too great to reliably separate NH from mild CHL, and AC ABR performed best. The ABR should remain the primary tool, and further ASSR research is needed.

Yoga, once separate from the fitness world, now offers many options for active people and athletes. Its benefits include breathing, meditation, concentration, flexibility, balance and injury prevention, which can enhance performance in sport and life. The many styles and Sanskrit terms can make choosing a class overwhelming, so the choice should depend on one's goals, needs and intention.

Hatha yoga is the umbrella term for posture-based styles. Popular classes include:

- **Ashtanga Vinyasa:** a demanding set sequence synchronized with breath.
- **Vinyasa/Flow:** breath-linked poses that vary by class.
- **Iyengar:** alignment-focused and therapeutic, using props.
- **Bikram/Hot Yoga:** 26 postures or flow sequences done in heated rooms.
- **Yin:** long-held poses that release connective tissue.
- **Restorative:** slow, prop-supported passive stretches.
- **Kripalu:** gentle and meditation-focused.

Specialty classes for runners, cyclists and other athletes address activity-specific stresses. Tight muscles from repetitive activities can cause imbalances, injuries and overuse syndrome. The author advises athletes who train hard to choose gentler, therapeutic styles and those needing balance to choose complementary practices, stressing that not all yoga is the same.

Heavens Fitness and Yoga Studio is hosting a free Outdoor Yoga Picnic on June 21 for International Yoga Day, accepting donations for Brown Bagging for Calgary Kids. The author, Helen Vanderburg, is a studio co-owner, fitness expert and author.

NVIDIA's Turing GPUs use a Hybrid Rendering model in which ray tracing and rasterization pipelines operate together, alongside AI and simulation, enabling real-time ray tracing on a single GPU.

**Ray Tracing and RT Cores**
- Each SM contains a new RT Core that accelerates Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) traversal and ray/triangle intersection testing.
- Without such hardware, these tasks require thousands of shader instruction slots per ray.
- RT Cores contain two units, one for bounding box tests and one for ray-triangle tests. They return hit/no-hit results, freeing the SM for other work.
- The driver handles BVH building and refitting. Applications manage ray generation and shading through new shader types.
- Turing delivers 10+ Giga Rays/Sec, about 10 times faster than Pascal's roughly 1.1 Giga Rays/Sec in software.
- Denoising reduces the number of rays needed per pixel.
- Supported APIs include RTX, OptiX, Microsoft DXR, and the upcoming Vulkan ray tracing API.
- Ray-traced shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections overcome limitations of shadow maps, SSAO, screen-space reflections, and cubemaps. Examples are shown from Battlefield V and Shadow of the Tomb Raider.

**NGX (Neural Graphics Acceleration)**
- NGX is a deep learning technology stack that uses Tensor Cores and does not work on pre-Turing GPUs.
- Pre-trained models are delivered through GeForce Experience or Quadro Experience.
- **DLSS:** Trained against 64x supersampled reference images, DLSS delivers quality similar to TAA with roughly half the shading work. This lets the RTX 2080 Ti achieve twice the GTX 1080 Ti's performance at 4K. DLSS 2X approaches 64xSS quality.
- **Other features:** InPainting, AI Slow-Mo, and AI Super Rez (2x–8x upscaling, running at about 30 fps for 1080p-to-4K).

**New Shading Features**
- **Mesh Shading:** Adds Task and Mesh Shaders that use a cooperative thread model. This removes CPU draw-call bottlenecks and enables level-of-detail selection and geometry manipulation.
- **Variable Rate Shading (VRS):** Allows a different shading rate for each 16x16 pixel region. It enables Content Adaptive Shading, Motion Adaptive Shading, and Foveated Rendering, and can increase shading rate with MSAA.
- **Texture Space Shading:** Decouples shading from screen-space visibility and allows reuse of shaded texels, for example in VR stereo rendering.
- **Multi-View Rendering:** Supports up to four views per pass in hardware and 32 at the API level, expanding on Pascal's SMP.
- **Resource binding:** Turing supports DX12 Tier 3 resource binding and Tier 2 resource heaps.

**VR**
- VirtualLink/USB Type-C provides a single-connector headset connection.
- MVR, foveated rendering, and RT Core-accelerated VRWorks Audio improve VR performance and immersion.

**Chips**
- **TU104** (RTX 2080, Tesla T4, Quadro RTX 5000): 13.6 billion transistors, 48 SMs, 3072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, 48 RT Cores, and second-generation NVLink.
- **Tesla T4:** Targets inference workloads with 2,560 CUDA Cores and 320 GB/s bandwidth.
- **TU106** (RTX 2070): 10.8 billion transistors, 2304 CUDA Cores, 36 RT Cores, and no NVLink or SLI support.

**RTX-OPS**
RTX-OPS is a workload-based metric that weights Tensor (20%), FP32 (80%), RT Core (40%), and INT32 (28%) operations. The RTX 2080 Ti rates at 78 RTX-OPS.

**Conclusion**
Hybrid rendering, denoising, BVH algorithms, and RT Cores together bring real-time ray tracing to graphics.

The Executive submits to Congress extracts from an agent's report on the political, military, and civil condition of Texas. The Executive has taken no steps to acknowledge Texas's independence, but explains its position because both Houses passed resolutions favoring recognition once Texas showed a functioning civil government.

Recognizing a state that has forcibly separated from another, which still claims it, is delicate. Premature recognition may be seen as unfriendly or as cause for war. The United States has consistently treated such matters as questions of fact, avoided interfering in other nations' internal disputes, and recognized prevailing parties only on clear evidence. Examples include Spain's former colonies, Mexico, New Granada, Venezuela, and Ecuador. The recognition power is not expressly delegated in the Constitution. Because it may lead to war, the Executive agrees, on grounds of expediency, that Congress should decide, without offering an opinion on strict constitutional authority.

Texas has expelled Mexican authority, defeated its army, and captured its chief. However, Mexico holds far greater force and threatens a new invasion, so Texan independence remains uncertain. Extra caution is warranted for several reasons:

* The United States once claimed Texas.
* Many Texans are American emigrants with shared language and principles.
* Texas has adopted a similar government.
* Texas intends to seek admission to the Union after recognition.

Early recognition could suggest the United States aims to acquire the territory. The Executive therefore advises waiting until Mexico or a major foreign power recognizes Texas, or until its sovereignty is proven. It pledges to cooperate with Congress if Congress decides otherwise.

Modeling nanoscale light-matter interactions is essential for quantum technologies such as quantum communications, photonic quantum computing, and quantum sensing. Classical Maxwell solvers cannot capture nonclassical features such as photon correlations or entanglement. Quantum models often describe idealized systems and cannot account for propagation and interference in realistic devices. Exact quantum formalisms do not couple naturally to Maxwell solvers and become computationally prohibitive. Semiclassical approximations cannot accurately capture non-classical photon statistics.

This motivates stochastic differential equations (SDEs), which are conventionally derived through phase-space representations, quantum trajectory methods, or quantum Langevin equations. The authors introduce an SDE approach that relies on none of these. It is a stochastic Bloch-vector method that links quantum emitter dynamics to classical electromagnetic fields and could be integrated with Maxwell solvers.

The method is validated against experiments using the Mollow spectrum, the triplet resonance fluorescence of a strongly driven two-level system. Stochastic trajectories of this system are coupled to a source current and propagated with a finite-difference time-domain solver.

Standard derivations yield a Fokker-Planck equation with a drift matrix and a symmetric, positive semidefinite diffusion matrix. This matrix is factorized to define the noise coupling in a linear Itô SDE. That symmetry restriction excludes asymmetric noise correlations arising from non-commuting operators. The authors overcome this by allowing a complex, non-symmetric diffusion matrix, interpreted as a noise cross-covariance between two coupled stochastic processes.

NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland operates the Glenn Extreme Environments Rig (GEER), the largest and most accurate simulator of conditions on other planets. It replicates Venus's surface atmosphere, temperature and pressure. After a record 80-day run, Case Western Reserve University graduate student Brandon Radoman-Shaw found that the conditions had radically altered the chemical make-up of his rock and mineral samples. Venus's dense, mostly carbon dioxide atmosphere forms a reactive supercritical fluid, and the planet also has lead-melting temperatures, pressures 100 times Earth's, and acid clouds.

Soviet probes in the 1970s survived only minutes to hours. A durable computer chip developed by a NASA team, including Phil Neudeck, operated for 21 days in GEER. It was the first multi-week electronics operation in a Venus environment, overcoming what was considered a mission's limiting factor.

Physicist Geoffrey Landis calls Venus "Earth's evil twin," shaped by a runaway greenhouse effect. He notes that the upper atmosphere is cooler and calmer, though its clouds are sulfuric acid. He says studying Venus can help predict Earth's climatic future and might reveal microbial life.

A study co-authored by Ian Stephen of Macquarie University found that women preferred the body odor of men who ate more fruits and vegetables, while men who ate many carbohydrates smelled less appealing. Researchers used a spectrophotometer to measure carotenoid levels in healthy young men's skin as an indicator of produce intake, and they collected food frequency questionnaires. Women then rated the sweat on T-shirts the men wore during exercise. Meat intake did not affect attractiveness but made odor more intense. This passage is from the SEV-ES Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) specification. It covers SEV-ES and SEV-SNP, which protect a guest's register state from the hypervisor by encrypting it during world switches. VMEXITs are classified as Automatic Exits (AE) or Non-Automatic Exits (NAE). For NAEs, the guest controls what state it exposes through the GHCB. The document standardizes the GHCB layout, the required NAE events and minimum exposed state, and special handling such as NMIs and SMP booting.

**GHCB structure and versions**
- The GHCB is a 4 KB decrypted page whose format mirrors the SEV-ES VMCB save state area.
- Version 2 adds initial SEV-SNP support and hypervisor feature advertisement through a 52-bit FEATURES bitmap.
- Revisions 2.01–2.04 add:
  - 64-bit guest request sequence numbers
  - new error codes
  - VLEK certificate GUIDs
  - APIC ID lists and multi-VMPL support
  - SEV-ES page state changes
  - the Confidential Computing Blob EFI protocol
  - SEV-TIO trusted device support
  - Secure AVIC
  - GHCB unregistration

**GHCB MSR protocol**
- The lower 12 bits of MSR 0xc001_0130 are used for requests before a GHCB is established. Requests include:
  - SEV information and version negotiation
  - CPUID values
  - AP reset hold
  - GHCB GPA registration, which is required for SEV-SNP
  - page state changes
  - Run VMPL
  - feature support
  - termination
- Negotiation examples are provided for SEV-ES and SEV-SNP guests.

**NAE handling**
- NAE events trigger a #VC exception. The guest copies the required state into the GHCB, sets VALID_BITMAP bits, and issues VMGEXIT.
- Interrupts and preemption should be disabled during GHCB use.
- Hypervisors report errors through the SW_EXITINFO1 and SW_EXITINFO2 fields.
- Specific events covered include:
  - IOIO, MSR, VMMCALL, and MMIO (#NPF)
  - page state change, using up to 253 entries with reason codes
  - SNP Guest Request and Extended Guest Request (certificates identified by GUID)
  - AP Creation
  - #HV doorbell page, IPI, and timer
  - APIC ID List, Run VMPL, and TIO Guest Request
  - Secure AVIC backing pages
  - termination

**Other topics**
- **SEV-ES identification:** Hypervisors must provide specific CPUID properties so a guest can detect it is running under SEV-ES.
- **SMP booting:** APs boot through AP reset hold and an AP jump table, or through the SNP AP Creation feature. AP Creation enables vCPU hotplug and is required under Restricted Injection.
- **NMIs:** The hypervisor intercepts #DB rather than IRET and waits for an "NMI Complete" message before injecting another NMI.
- **Debug registers:** Hardware debug registers can be virtualized via DebugVirtualization. Otherwise, the guest caches DR7 values.
- **Unsupported features:** SMM and nested virtualization are not supported.

**SNP Restricted Injection**
- The host signals the guest only through #HV doorbells.
- The shared doorbell page contains a PendingEvent field (interrupt vector, NMI, #MC, and NoFurtherSignal bits) and a NoEoiRequired field.
- Guests execute HLT with interrupts disabled.
- The host must faithfully emulate APIC interrupt presentation, acknowledgment, and EOI semantics.

Human rights education (HRE) spans all stages of learning, yet in universities it remains largely confined to law schools, even though human rights principles run through many disciplines. Established teaching models predate contemporary threats such as climate change, refugee crises, disinformation, inequality and artificial intelligence. They also predate efforts to decolonise the curriculum. Fewer HRE guides exist for higher education than for schools.

HRE still centres on international human rights law and avoids sensitive historical cases. This runs counter to its purpose, but such material can also retraumatise students. Over half of UK university students have experienced adverse childhood experiences, and many carry lived or intergenerational trauma. Groups at heightened risk include LGBTQ+ students and refugees.

Trauma-informed HRE (TIHRE) aims to reduce harm, empower learners as survivors rather than victims, and move them from apathy to advocacy. The article draws on a structured, interdisciplinary literature review and SAMHSA's six principles:

- safety
- trustworthiness and transparency
- peer support
- collaboration
- empowerment and choice
- recognition of cultural, historical and gender issues

It makes three recommendations:

1. **Teaching persona:** Educators should undertake values clarification and "locate" themselves to identify biases, privilege and unresolved trauma. They should build an authentic teaching persona grounded in community, capability and confidence. Learning students' names also helps build trust.

2. **Content design:** Courses should integrate the UN framework of learning about, through and for human rights. Recommended practices include:
   - project-based learning, student co-creation and skills development
   - avoiding graphic material, "trauma porn" and romanticised trauma or resilience
   - giving content warnings and holding wellbeing check-ins
   - using reflective models such as Gibbs' Reflective Cycle

3. **Dialogic learning:** Drawing on Freire, teaching should rest on horizontal, trust-based relationships that build critical thinking and advocacy skills. Learners should also engage with survivors and practitioners, including through virtual guest speakers, which the article notes is underused in UK higher education.

Overall, trauma-informed practice should place wellbeing, agency and dignity at the centre of human rights teaching.

This paper by Wu, Akin, Martineau, Grégoire, and Veneris (ICAIF '25) examines whether the textual "soft" content of earnings press releases predicts stock returns on earnings announcement days, alongside "hard" information (earnings surprises relative to analyst forecasts). The authors note that press releases have received less research attention than conference calls, despite being released first, widely disseminated, and targeted in documented hacking incidents.

**Data and methods**
- The study uses over 138,000 press releases from SEC 8-K filings (2005–2023), covering more than 6,000 firms, with 134,354 releases from 2006–2023 in the main analysis.
- Text is vectorized using five methods:
  - Bag-of-words topic models: the BKMX taxonomy and online LDA (oLDA), with GPT-4o used to label topics.
  - BERT-family embeddings: BERT, MPNET, and FinBERT.
- Lasso regression in a rolling annual window generates return scores while avoiding look-ahead bias.
- Predictive power is assessed with cross-sectional regressions and SHAP values.

**Findings**
- **Explanatory power:** Earnings surprise alone explains 3.3% of announcement-day return variation. Adding soft information raises this to 4.4% with FinBERT, which performs best. In that model, the SHAP importance of text (52%) slightly exceeds that of surprise (48%), so soft and hard information are roughly equally informative.
- **Leakage:** Soft information does not explain returns the day before announcements, suggesting low likelihood of press release leakage.
- **Topic analysis:** Managers frame internal factors, such as financial performance and metrics, positively and external factors, such as sector and market conditions, negatively. The authors interpret this as consistent with self-serving bias. oLDA and FinBERT offer the greatest interpretability.
- **Market efficiency:** A long-short strategy entered at 9:45 a.m. after overnight releases yields negative, near-zero returns, mainly reflecting transaction costs. This indicates prices fully incorporate the information by market open.
- **Advance access:** If press release content and surprises were available beforehand, combining agreeing signals raises precision in identifying the top 10 best- and worst-performing stocks from 0.25–0.36 to 0.44–0.52. The authors say this underscores the need for newswire cybersecurity.

Future work will incorporate conference call text and audio.

This IDC White Paper examines how manufacturers use IT-based simulation, modeling, and data analysis, and the role of high-performance computing (HPC) in these calculations. It draws on a December 2021 telephone survey of 200 IT and departmental decision makers at discrete and process manufacturers with more than 500 employees in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland.

**Context and goals**
Manufacturers face geopolitical uncertainty, rising energy prices, raw material and skilled labor shortages, supply chain disruptions, and sustainability pressures. Digitalization is also changing how they create value. Respondents link simulation, modeling, and analysis to key business goals:
- Three-quarters consider increasing innovation most important.
- 57% see these tools as a way to improve quality and avoid defects.

**Current and planned use**
- About half already use these tools in product development and in production and process planning.
- Deployment in each of these areas is expected to reach up to 90% within two years.
- 64% plan related investments.

IDC identifies data silos as an obstacle and recommends a unified "single source of the truth." Other key applications include:
- Virtual prototyping
- Digital twins
- Design optimization
- Digital verification and validation
- High-performance data analytics, already used by 42%

Bridgestone reports that tire digital twins can cut development time by up to 50%.

**Demand for computing power**
- Increasingly complex calculations force trade-offs between time and accuracy.
- 42% of respondents use outdated or inaccurate simulations.
- Half say iterations take too long.
- Only 8% currently report high demand for high-performance calculations, but almost half expect to within two years.

**HPC as a game changer**
81% of respondents view HPC as a game changer for product and process innovation, rising to 96% among those that have implemented it. The paper says HPC:
- Enables complex calculations
- Improves quality and intensity of use
- Unlocks new usage scenarios
- Increases agility

More than a quarter of enterprises use HPC, 39% are planning or piloting it, and 15% are not engaging with it.

**HPC environments and challenges**
- 87% of HPC users prefer or plan external infrastructure.
- 74% use or plan colocation.
- 43% use or plan research institutions.
- Only 6% run on-premises HPC.

The main challenges are:
- Security concerns (72%)
- High investment and licensing costs
- Energy consumption and sustainability (58%)

This study evaluates strategies for extending Universal Interatomic Potentials (UIPs), which are mostly trained on bulk data, to material surfaces. Bulk-trained UIPs tend to underestimate surface energies. The authors compare four approaches:

- **TS**: training from scratch on surface data
- **ZS**: zero-shot use of a pre-trained UIP
- **FT**: fine-tuning the UIP
- **MHFT**: multi-head fine-tuning, which trains on bulk and surface data together

After benchmarking several UIPs on diatomic potential curves, MACE-MP-0a-small was chosen as the foundation model.

**Gold (unary):** Fine-tuning with only 40 configurations reduced ZS errors from 14.8 meV/atom and 74.7 meV/Å to 4.3 meV/atom and 37.4 meV/Å. TS trained on 2,000 configurations performed similarly to or worse than FT trained on 40–200. The TS model produced unrealistic Au–Au diatomic behavior at short and long range, which was attributed to missing close-range pairs in the training data.

**RuO₂ (binary):** FT again outperformed TS, although force errors were several times larger than for gold. The TS model showed unphysical O–O potential minima. FT showed a spurious region below 0.4 Å, but it lies behind a ~500 eV barrier.

**BiVO₄ (ternary):** FT achieved the lowest force RMSE (0.17 eV/Å) with three outliers above 4 eV/Å. TS had a lower RMSE than ZS (0.24 vs. 0.42 eV/Å) but more outliers (13 vs. 2). The authors attribute TS's failures to insufficient training on high-force environments.

**Multi-head fine-tuning:** Fine-tuning on gold degraded predictions for Ag, Cu, Pt, and Ir surfaces and caused catastrophic forgetting on bulk MPTrj data. Surface-energy RMSEs were 27 (ZS), 88 (FT), and 16 (MHFT) meV/Å². On MPTrj bulk data, energy errors were 11 (foundation), 302 (FT), and 27 (MHFT) meV/atom. MHFT slightly reduced gold accuracy (2.8 vs. 1 meV/atom) and required roughly 100 times more training time.

**Conclusions:** FT reaches comparable accuracy with far less data and gives more physically realistic potentials. Performance declines as system complexity increases. MHFT preserves bulk accuracy and improves out-of-domain predictions, but it requires aligned computational conditions between datasets, whereas FT tolerates moderate variations. Calculations used MACE 0.3.12 and VASP 6.5.0 with PBE.

Amsterdam's Buiksloterham docklands regeneration is an experimental project focused on localisation, sustainability and circular living. It minimises waste through a wormery, composting toilets and a struvite reactor that turns urine into fertiliser, with compost used to grow food for its cafe. Backtests of the RSI indicator, which measures the speed and magnitude of price movements on a 0–100 scale, found it works on Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies as a momentum indicator but not as a mean reversion indicator. Buying low RSI readings and selling high ones, which has worked on US equities, produced weak results on Bitcoin from January 2015 to September 2021. The best-performing variation had only three trades, and profit factors dropped as trade counts rose. Ethereum and Doge showed similar results. In contrast, momentum strategies performed much better. Buying when the five-day RSI crossed above 50 and selling when it fell below 50 yielded a 122% CAGR versus 101% for buy and hold, with a 39% drawdown versus 83%. Ethereum and Doge also showed good momentum results.

The MACD-histogram trading strategy is a mean-reversion system that identifies momentum changes and reversal points. Tested on 77 liquid ETFs, it generated 6,669 trades. Entry is on the close, and exit is on the first day the close is higher than the previous close. Long positions perform much better than short positions. Since 2000, almost none of the ETFs show a negative average gain per trade. The strategy is in cash most of the time.

A backtest on QLD (2x Nasdaq 100) since 2007 produced 85 trades, an average gain of 2.2%, 10.4% annual returns, and a 19% maximum drawdown, while invested only 5% of the time. The MACD histogram shows the difference between the MACD and signal lines. Bars above zero indicate bullish momentum, and bars below zero indicate bearish momentum.

SpinGPT is a large-language-model agent for Spin & Go, a three-player hyper-turbo poker tournament. Tournament play differs from the two-player cash games where most poker AI progress, largely based on Counterfactual Regret Minimization (CFR), has occurred. Player counts and stack sizes change, and chip value is non-linear.

**Model and training**
- SpinGPT is built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and trained in two stages.
- **Supervised fine-tuning (SpinGPT-SFT):** The first stage used LoRA on 320,000 decisions from 8,800 high-stakes Spin & Go games played professionally by co-author Narada Maugin on PartyPoker.fr (2018–2020). Hands were encoded as structured text prompts, with actions output as compact tokens.
- **Offline reinforcement learning:** The second stage applied ORPO to 270,000 synthetic post-flop hands from the CFR-based solver InstaGTO, plus 50,000 retained human hands to prevent catastrophic forgetting.

**Results**
- **SpinGPT-SFT:** On professional data, it achieved 80% exact accuracy and an 86% macro F1 score, compared with 78% macro F1 for PokerGPT. It produced 1.4% illegal moves.
- **Final SpinGPT on professional data:** Accuracy dipped slightly to 79%, interpreted as a shift away from pure imitation. Bet-sizing error (MAE) improved from 0.61 to 0.30 BB.
- **Final SpinGPT on solver data:** It reached 72% exact and 78% tolerant accuracy.
- **Against Slumbot:** With a heuristic patch replacing all-in bets, which were excessive at 200 BB stacks, SpinGPT-SFT won 13.4 ± 12.9 BB/100 over 30,000 hands.
- **Head-to-head:** The final SpinGPT beat SpinGPT-SFT by 13.2 ± 7.24 BB/100 over 10,000 duplicate hands.

**Limitations and future work**
- The final model was not tested against Slumbot, and the benchmark format is mismatched.
- Language-model errors occurred, such as treating 5.11 as greater than 5.2.
- Total compute was estimated at 5.2 kgCO2e.
- Proposed future work includes stronger base models, retrieval of GTO charts, chain-of-thought reasoning, opponent adaptivity, natural-language explanations, and coupling the LLM with a solver.

This manuscript illustrates the value of critical approaches to quantitative research in education and offers epistemological and methodological guidance. Its audience includes student researchers, faculty, institutional researchers, and methods instructors.

**Positionalities**
The authors argue that quantitative research has never been objective and that researchers' positionalities are inherent to scholarship.
- **Jay**, a white, queer, cisgender scholar, studies queer and trans collegians and the invisibility of these students in survey design.
- **Jimmy**, a Vietnamese-Chinese American institutional researcher, highlights how aggregating "Asian/Asian American" data masks inequalities and perpetuates the model minority myth.

**Quantitative Criticalism**
Quantitative criticalism combines quantitative methods with critical epistemologies to advance social justice and challenge oppressive systems. It holds that numbers are not neutral and that criticality must run through every research stage. It also emphasizes:
- solidarity among scholars
- community partnership
- data sovereignty
- transparent authorship

**Tensions**
- Statistics originated in white supremacist and eugenic logic, notably through Galton and Pearson.
- The "threshold" of criticality is undefined, partly because authors' intentions are hard to discern.
- Surveys rely on essentialist identity variables.
- Small samples of multiply minoritized groups limit analyses, and nonparametric methods are underused in curricula.
- Valid measures of systemic oppression are difficult to build.
- Generalizability rests on post-positivist assumptions that center white norms.

The authors view these tensions as potentially generative.

**Examples**
- **Critical Race Theory:** Sablan (2019) used a QuantCrit approach to operationalize Yosso's community cultural wealth model into four scales. The study is limited by its narrow population.
- **Queer Theory:** Garvey (2017) advocated including "queer" as a survey option and testing within-group differences, while acknowledging that categorization contradicts queer theory.
- **Intersectionality:** Szymanski and Lewis (2016) used interaction effects to study African American women's coping with gendered racism, but relied on measures not designed for this population. Wilson and Urick (2022) used latent class analysis. No consensus exists on how best to integrate intersectionality.

**Implications and Closing**
The authors reject claims of expertise and view criticality as a continuum. However, they also note that incremental change can serve white supremacy. They pose questions to readers about their intentions, whether white supremacist methods can serve liberation, and their own threshold of criticality. They conclude that quantitative methods lacking epistemological grounding are insufficient and call for a coalition centering critical reflection.

Implementing clinical practice guidelines is difficult, especially in intensive care units, where patient data are complex and voluminous. This study evaluated the accuracy and efficiency of an automated system for monitoring guideline adherence. The system combines Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) for computer-interpretable guideline representation with the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model for patient data.

**Methods**
- From 41 intensive care guidelines with 1,597 recommendations, experts selected six, mostly COVID-19-related, covering:
  - prophylactic anticoagulation
  - avoiding therapeutic anticoagulation
  - tidal volume
  - PEEP
  - prone positioning
  - sepsis tidal volume
- The recommendations were encoded in FHIR and validated by specialists.
- Data from five university hospitals, each using different information systems, were transformed into the OMOP CDM through hospital-specific ETL pipelines.
- An execution engine queried the patient data to determine each recommendation's applicability and adherence, using data from January 2020 to May 2023.
- In three hospitals, seven intensive care physicians manually reviewed selected days.
- Two experienced supervising physicians established the ground truth for disagreements.

**Results**
- The dataset covered 82,015 intensive care episodes.
- The system achieved 97.0% accuracy, compared with 86.6% for human reviewers (p < 0.001). It also showed higher specificity, precision and F1 score.
- Human review took about 30 seconds per patient, day and recommendation. The system evaluated more than 2,000 patient days per second.
- Over 80% of discrepancies were human errors, arising from overlooked data and inconsistent interpretation of imprecise recommendations.
- System errors stemmed mainly from unstructured free-text data that was not transferred to the OMOP CDM.
- Adherence varied by recommendation and hospital, mostly ranging from 10% to 60%. Contributing factors included:
  - the novelty of the COVID-19 recommendations
  - incomplete documentation
  - strict evaluation criteria
  - imprecise recommendation wording

**Recommendations**
The authors recommend that guidelines explicitly define tolerance ranges, adherence frequency or duration, acceptable deviation limits, and relevant measurement time intervals.

**Limitations**
- The validation was retrospective.
- The expert ground truth may contain bias.
- Only a limited number of recommendations were assessed.

**Conclusion**
The system provides scalable, accurate and efficient guideline adherence monitoring across institutions.

A 2018 Journal of Climate paper by Nicholas Lewis and Judith Curry concludes that the high warming estimates from most computer climate simulations are inconsistent with observed warming since 1850. This implies future warming 30 to 45% lower than the simulations suggest. The study estimates climate sensitivity from observed temperature changes and estimates of greenhouse gas and other climate drivers from the mid/late 19th century to 2016. It uses IPCC AR5 forcing estimates, updated with recent revisions and extended to 2016.

Using globally-complete temperature data, the study derives median estimates of:

- **Equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS):** 1.66°C, compared with 3.1°C for 31 CMIP5 models. Allowing for time-varying feedbacks raises this to 1.76°C.
- **Transient climate response (TCR):** 1.33°C, compared with 1.9°C for the CMIP5 models.

These estimates are slightly lower than those of a predecessor study and have much lower upper uncertainty bounds. They imply future warming of only 55–70% of the central CMIP5 projection. The estimates were largely insensitive to the analysis period chosen.

The paper finds previous methodological criticisms unfounded. Potential biases from forcing efficacy, sea-surface warming patterns and temperature estimation were found to be minor when using globally-complete data. Lewis states that future warming is likely to be substantially lower than the IPCC's central model-simulated projection.

This patent application, a divisional in a chain of related filings, describes methods for forming 3-dimensional vertical NOR-type (VNOR) memory string arrays using damascene local vertical bit lines.

**Core method and ribboning avoidance:** Local word lines are etched in two steps to avoid "ribboning," a stress-induced deformation of narrow, tall features. A memory structure of multi-layers (e.g., silicon nitride and silicon oxide) is formed above global interconnect lines on a semiconductor substrate. A first set of trenches is etched and filled with sacrificial dielectric. A second mask then defines parallel trenches, forming narrow word line stacks. Using wider masks reduces the etch aspect ratio. For example, a 50 nm wide, 2,000 nm tall stack has a 40:1 ratio, while a 180 nm mask yields about 11:1. Lithographic misalignment can cause unequal word line widths. This variability can be handled in chip design by grouping left- and right-side transistors with dedicated reference transistors.

**Word line and transistor formation:**
- **Word lines:** Silicon nitride layers are selectively removed. The sacrificial dielectric supports the stacks while the resulting cavities are filled with metal (e.g., TiN and tungsten) to form word lines.
- **Memory layers:** Vias are etched in two rounds. In each, tunneling dielectric, charge storage, blocking dielectric, channel, optional liner and sacrificial dielectric layers are deposited conformally.
- **Source and drain:** Shafts are etched and filled with heavily doped semiconductor to form common source regions connected to the lower global interconnect lines. Drain regions (bit lines) are formed similarly but connect to a second set of global interconnect lines above the structure.
- **Transistors:** Thin-film transistors form where word line strips overlap the channel and storage layers.

**Interconnect options:** Some source or drain conductors may connect directly to substrate circuitry. Alternatively, one set of global interconnect lines may be eliminated if the remaining set has roughly half the pitch.

**Word line contacts:** Word lines are contacted through a staircase structure formed by successive mask recessing and etching, followed by dielectric fill and conductive vias.

**Alternative embodiments:**
- Dielectric pillars, formed before word line patterning, provide mechanical support to the stacks.
- Stacked masks of differing pitch define the word line stacks.

Arizona has long led U.S. school choice, with open enrollment, charter schools, a private school tax credit, and, in 2011, the nation's first Empowerment Scholarship Account (ESA) vouchers. It later became the first state to make ESAs universal, in 2022, after voters had rejected a capped expansion in 2018. The state provides over $1 billion annually in subsidies to private education. Citing a lack of accountability and transparency, the Grand Canyon Institute (GCI) compiles its past research and adds new analysis.

**Enrollment and funding**
- ESA enrollment grew from 144 in FY2012 to 12,127 in FY2022, then to 87,602 by FY2025's third quarter.
- Of that total, 64,133 are universal and 15,207 qualify through K-12 disability.
- Vouchers equal 90% of charter school funding. Most awards are under $8,000, though some exceed $30,000.

**FY2023 spending**
- GCI estimates $304 million was spent.
- $173 million went to private schools: 51% to religious schools (86% of that to Evangelical Christian and Catholic schools), 44% to special needs schools, and under 5% to secular schools.
- Private school tuition covered less than 40% of student enrollment quarters, suggesting many families use ESAs for homeschooling or extracurriculars.
- Unspent balances reached $175 million across about 60,000 accounts. GCI estimates they grew to $360 million by the end of FY2024.
- GCI's records requests for FY2024 data have been denied or remain pending.

**Who participates**
- In 2022, 45% of universal applicants came from the wealthiest zip codes, and 80% were not in public school.
- From May 2023 to March 2025, participation rose from 2.6% to 4.4% in low-income zip codes and from 7.7% to 10.9% in very high-income zip codes. The income gap has narrowed but persists.

**Net cost**
- Transfers from charter schools produce modest state savings. Transfers from district schools add costs, and students who never attended public schools represent the full voucher cost.
- About 90% of FY2025 new universal entrants came from district or charter schools, half of them from charters.
- Nearly three-quarters of all universal participants never attended public schools.
- GCI estimates the net cost at least $332 million in FY2024 and about $350 million in FY2025.

**Mega Geometry**
Mega Geometry is a new RTX technology that lets ray-traced applications, including engines such as Unreal Engine 5 with Nanite, ray trace geometry at full fidelity without low-resolution proxies. It consists of new API extensions, a driver implementation, and Blackwell RT Core optimizations. It addresses two challenges:
- **Cluster-based LOD updates:** Cluster-level Acceleration Structures (CLAS) treat batches of up to 256 triangles as primitives. CLAS can be cached and used to build BVHs, cutting processing by two orders of magnitude. The APIs are fully batched and GPU-driven, which nearly eliminates CPU overhead for BVH management.
- **High object counts:** A Partitioned Top-Level Acceleration Structure (PTLAS) updates only the partitions that have changed, rather than rebuilding the TLAS every frame.

Mega Geometry also enables fast ray tracing of animated, displaced subdivision surfaces by mapping tessellation to cluster generation. It is supported in DirectX 12 (via NVAPI), Vulkan, and OptiX 9.0, on all RTX GPUs from Turing onward. Blackwell's 4th-generation RT Cores add cluster engines with geometry and BVH compression and up to 2x the ray-triangle intersection rate, reducing VRAM use in Nanite scenes by several hundred MB.

**Linear Swept Spheres (LSS)**
Blackwell RT Cores add hardware intersection testing for LSS, a primitive built from spheres swept along linear segments. It is used for hair, fur, and similar strands, and also supports standalone spheres for particles. Compared to Disjoint Orthogonal Triangle Strips (DOTS), LSS renders human hair about 2x faster and uses about 5x less VRAM.

**SER 2.0**
Shader Execution Reordering reorganizes GPU threads to improve utilization in divergent workloads and neural shading. On Blackwell, its reorder logic is twice as efficient and more precise. Existing applications that use SER benefit without code changes.

**AI Management Processor (AMP)**
AMP is a dedicated RISC-V context scheduler that offloads GPU scheduling from the CPU. It aligns with Windows Hardware-Accelerated GPU Scheduling and reduces latency and stuttering when AI and graphics workloads run concurrently.

**Video and Display**
- Blackwell adds hardware encode and decode for 4:2:2 chroma-sampled video, which offers 2x the color information of 4:2:0 for 1.3x the file size.
- The 9th-generation NVENC improves AV1 and HEVC quality by 5% BD-BR PSNR and adds an AV1 UHQ mode, for up to 15% combined improvement.
- The RTX 5090 has three encoders and two decoders, giving over 50% faster exports than the previous generation.
- The 6th-generation NVDEC doubles H.264 decode speed.
- DisplayPort 2.1b supports up to 80 Gbps, enabling 8K at 165Hz and 4K at 480Hz with DSC.

**Max-Q Power Efficiency**
- **Advanced Power Gating:** Finer clock, power, and rail gating, including full memory clock-tree gating and a separate voltage rail for cores and memory.
- **Accelerated Frequency Switching:** Clocks adjust to workloads 1000x faster than before.
- **Low Latency Sleep:** The deepest sleep state is entered 10x faster than on Ada.
- Together, these yield up to 50% power savings in small language model inference.

**DLSS 4**
- **Multi Frame Generation:** Generates up to three frames per rendered frame using a model that is 40% faster and uses 30% less VRAM. Frame pacing is handled by hardware Flip Metering in the display engine.
- **Transformer models:** These replace CNNs for Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and DLAA. They use twice the parameters and improve temporal stability, motion detail, and lighting while reducing ghosting.

**Neural Shaders**
Blackwell is designed for neural shaders, in which AI models approximate traditional shader computations. The Cooperative Vectors API for DX12 and Vulkan, developed with Microsoft, exposes Tensor Cores to any shader type. Applications include:
- **RTX Neural Materials:** Film-quality materials at game frame rates; one demo used 333 MB instead of 1110 MB.
- **Neural Texture Compression:** Up to 7:1 compression over block-compressed formats, aided by Stochastic Texture Filtering.
- **Neural Radiance Cache:** Infers multi-bounce indirect lighting from rays traced for one bounce.
- **RTX Skin:** The first ray-traced subsurface scattering in games.
- **RTX Neural Faces:** A generative AI model that infers more natural-looking faces.
